concept.name: Risk tolerance
concept.definition: The amount of risk an individual or organization is willing to accept in pursuit of its objectives. In the ISO 31000 risk vocabulary, willingness (appetite/tolerance in the willingness sense) is distinguished from capacity - what the entity is able to bear - and from the risk threshold, the point at which action to reduce risk is required.
concept.intuition: Risk tolerance is how much drawdown you can stomach without abandoning the plan - a psychological willingness number, not a financial one.
concept.mechanics: Assessed through questionnaires, drawdown history, and observed behavior under loss, then translated into concrete constraints: per-trade risk, position-size limits, and portfolio volatility targets. It is meant to be set in advance and revisited on a schedule, not discovered mid-drawdown.
concept.failure_modes: Stated tolerance is systematically overestimated in bull markets and after wins, and is revealed only in drawdowns - willingness expressed at the top rarely survives contact with a real loss. Questionnaires also conflate tolerance with capacity and with recent experience.
concept.misconceptions: Risk tolerance is not fixed by personality alone, and it is not the same as risk capacity: a wealthy investor can have low tolerance, while a leveraged investor can report high tolerance yet have almost no capacity. Feeling comfortable with risk is not evidence you can afford it.
concept.example: A trader states he can tolerate a 30% drawdown but starts breaking rules at -12%; his revealed tolerance, not the questionnaire answer, should drive position sizing.
